Settings

Features

Toggle features without a redeploy. A toggle here overrides the matching env var (VOTING_ENABLED, REACTIONS_ENABLED, …); "Reset to defaults" clears the overrides so the env vars / built-in defaults apply again.

Display & pagination

Control how many comments load at once and how nested replies collapse. Smaller values keep a busy thread from pushing the rest of the page down.

Comments per page Top-level comments shown per initial load. "Load older comments" reveals the next batch.
Replies before “show more” Replies shown under each comment before a “Show N more replies” button. 0 = show all.
Auto-collapse depth Replies nested at this depth or deeper start collapsed. 0 = never auto-collapse.
Default order Order top-level comments load in. Readers can still switch order themselves; this is only where they start. "Top" needs voting enabled — with voting off it serves newest first instead, and your choice here is kept for if you turn voting back on.
Language Language for the widget, the Atom feed and notification emails. Comment text is never translated. An embed can override this per-page with data-lang. "Follow the page" reads the host page's <html lang> — reviewed translations only, so a machine-translated language has to be chosen here or on the embed.

Moderation

The edit window, thread auto-close and community auto-collapse. Auto-close and auto-collapse are off by default. Closing a thread only blocks new comments — existing ones stay visible and votes/reactions stay live. Auto-collapse just folds heavily-downvoted comments; readers can still expand them.

Edit window (minutes) How long after posting an author may still revise their own comment. 0 = no editing at all.
Auto-close after (days) Close a thread to new comments this many days after the article's publish date (or, if the host page doesn't send one, the first comment's date). 0 = never auto-close by age. Existing comments stay visible.
Auto-collapse: minimum votes A comment needs at least this many total votes before the downvote ratio can collapse it. Guards new comments from being folded by a single downvote. Ignored when the ratio below is 0.
Auto-collapse: downvote % Fold a comment (readers can still expand it) once this percent of its votes are downvotes and it has met the minimum above. 0 = never auto-collapse. Needs downvotes enabled.
Close all threads on Instance-wide sunset: once this date passes, no thread accepts new comments. Leave empty to disable. Takes effect within a few minutes of the date passing.

Anti-spam heuristics

Cheap local checks that run before the (optional, paid) classifier. A tripped check never drops a comment — it routes it to the queue, so tune these while watching what lands there. The classifier provider and its API keys stay in wrangler.toml; see the Configuration tab.

Link threshold Queue a comment carrying more than this many links. -1 = check off; 0 = queue anything with a link at all.
Minimum fill time (ms) Queue a comment submitted faster than this after the form loaded — bots post instantly, people don't. 0 = check off.

Fill-time check is inactive. It needs SPAM_FORM_TS_SECRET to sign the form timestamp — without it an unsigned time is trivially forged, so the check is skipped. Set the secret with wrangler secret put SPAM_FORM_TS_SECRET and redeploy.

Muted words One term per line. A bare term matches whole words only, so ass does not flag "class"; wrap it in * to match anywhere (*casino*) or trail one for a prefix (t.me/*). Case-insensitive, and lookalike forms (ｖｉａｇｒａ) and zero-width characters are folded away — but accents are kept and leetspeak is not decoded. This is not a regex: . and ( are literal. Lines starting with # are comments. Checked against the comment body, author name and page URL. A hit sends the comment to the queue; nothing is ever silently dropped. Up to 200 terms, 100 characters and 4 wildcards each — a term over those limits is skipped, the rest of the list still applies.

term(s). Only the first 200 are checked — the rest are ignored.

Clearing the box saves an empty list, which is not the same as never having set one: it overrides whatever SPAM_BLOCKLIST your deploy ships. "Reset to defaults" is the way back to that.

Confirmation-email ceiling

A hard cap on how much subscription-confirmation mail this instance will send, counted globally rather than per reader. It exists because the other two limits on that endpoint can both be walked past by an attacker cycling email addresses, so this is the one that holds — at the cost of being shared: a spent window turns away genuine new subscribers until it rolls. Already-confirmed subscribers and their digests are never affected. Denials are logged, so watch wrangler tail before assuming these need raising.

Confirmation emails per minute (global) Total subscription-confirmation emails this instance will send in any 60-second window, across all readers. Raise it if a post gets busy enough that genuine subscribers see "too many requests" — the log line to look for in `wrangler tail` is `confirmation email budget exhausted`. Cannot be set to 0: a 0 ceiling silently breaks all new subscriptions rather than disabling the check.
Confirmation emails per day (global) Same counter over a 24-hour window. The default 200 sits deliberately above Resend's free-tier 100/day, so your mail provider's limit is what a normal instance meets first. Lower it below 100 (minus your expected digest volume) if you'd rather Garrul stop sending before your provider starts rejecting.

Privacy retention

Garrul stores a keyed hash of the commenter's IP (never the address itself) so you can spot a ban evader on the same network and dedupe abuse reports. Retention puts an expiry on that: past the window, the cron erases the hash and user-agent from comments and reports, so a database export carries a bounded slice of history instead of everything the instance has ever seen. Off by default.

Clear stored IP hashes after (days) Erase the hashed IP and user-agent on comments and reports once they're this old. 0 = keep them for the life of the row (the default). Values from 1 to 6 are ignored — the sweep refuses anything under 7 days so a typo can't wipe nearly everything. Irreversible: a cleared hash is gone, and with it the ability to spot a ban evader on that network. Anonymous ghost accounts are never swept — their hash is the identity itself.
Delete audit-log rows after (days) Prune the moderation audit trail once entries are this old. 0 = keep it forever (the default). Values from 1 to 29 are ignored — the sweep refuses anything under 30 days, a higher floor than the IP one because a moderation record stays useful for months. Irreversible, and whole rows go rather than being redacted: an audit entry with the actor stripped out reads as evidence while proving nothing. Set this if "we keep moderation records indefinitely" is a retention period you'd rather not have to justify.

This one can't be undone. Setting the window back to 0 stops future sweeps; it does not restore what a sweep already erased. Watch it run, and drain a backlog on demand, from Operator.

Vulnerability disclosure

Where a security researcher should report a vulnerability in this instance. When set, it is published at /.well-known/security.txt (RFC 9116), the standard place researchers look. Unset, that route answers 404.

Disclosure contact An email address, or an https:// or mailto: URI. Anything else is treated as unset. Empty (the default) keeps the route a 404 — the file is only served once there is a real contact behind it.
